short: One legion, one river, and the end of the Roman Republic.
full:
On 10 January 49 BCE Julius Caesar led the Thirteenth Legion across the Rubicon, the stream marking the boundary between his province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper. Roman law forbade a provincial commander from bringing troops into Italy; doing so was treason. The Senate, pressed by Pompey and by Caesar's enemies, had demanded he give up his army. Suetonius records the remark alea iacta est - the die is cast.

Civil war followed immediately. Pompey abandoned Rome and withdrew to Greece, was beaten at Pharsalus in 48 BCE and murdered in Egypt. Caesar defeated the remaining Pompeians in Africa and Spain, was made dictator for life, and was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE. The Republic did not recover: after thirteen more years of civil war his heir Octavian emerged as sole ruler and became Augustus. The phrase survives in English for a step that cannot be undone. Sabaton's "Crossing the Rubicon", from Legends (2025), takes the moment as its subject.
